introduction: “The cause of motion is heat, and the cause of heat is the Word of God.” In the Tablet of Wisdom Bahá’u’lláh, writing to a believer trained in the old philosophy, says that the world came to be through heat generated between an active force and its recipient, and that the heat itself came from the Word. The other readings repeat and apply the formula. In physics: heat is latent in things and is released as motion; atoms never rest; nothing is lost, only converted. In the soul: the love of God is the heat that sets a person moving, and a community without it comes to a standstill. The outside quotations follow both lines. Heraclitus made fire and flux the nature of the world, Aristotle described the elements changing into one another, Bacon identified heat with motion, and Lavoisier stated the conservation the fourth reading assumes. For the inward sense there is the psalmist whose heart grew hot until he spoke, Jeremiah’s fire in the bones, and Psalm 147, where God’s word melts the ice and the waters flow. Aristotle’s unmoved mover and the psalm’s “be still” are set beside the reading that calls God both Stillness and Motion.
questions: “The test of existence is motion.” By this test, where is your own life most alive, and where has it stopped?
The readings use one law for physics and for the soul: heat causes motion. How far can such a parallel be pressed? What does it explain, and what would it be a mistake to conclude from it?
“The cause of heat is the Word of God.” What has warmed you enough to make you act?
“He Who is both Stillness and Motion.” What place has stillness in a life of the kind these readings describe?

outside.why: “The world of existence came into being through the heat generated from the interaction between the active force and that which is its recipient.” Heraclitus: this world was ever, is now, and ever shall be an ever-living Fire.

The two “are the same, yet they are different.” Aristotle, in the tradition the Tablet addresses: all of them are by nature such as to change into one another: for coming-to-be is a change into contraries and out of contraries.
The reading traces that heat to the Word of God. John: in the beginning was the Word; all things were made by him.
Heat is latent in all things, and a power makes it manifest; so with love in hearts. The psalmist: my heart was hot within me, while I was musing the fire burned: then spake I with my tongue.
“The test of existence is motion.” Paul at Athens: in him we live, and move, and have our being.
“If motion is withheld growth ceases.” Tennyson’s Ulysses: how dull it is to pause, to make an end, to rust unburnish’d, not to shine in use!
Warmth is latent in wood and is released by friction: “a conversion into power.” Bacon reached the modern view of heat in 1620: heat itself, its essence and quiddity, is Motion and nothing else.
“There is no qualitative” change, only conversion. Lavoisier: in all the operations of art and nature, nothing is created; an equal quantity of matter exists both before and after the experiment.
“Ascent and descent, stillness and motion, have come into being through the will of the Lord.” Heraclitus: the way up and the way down is one and the same.
“The fire of the love of God … will become the cause of ascension and the reason for motion.” Jeremiah: his word was in mine heart as a burning fire shut up in my bones, and I could not stay.
Two disciples, set on the road again by a conversation: did not our heart burn within us?
Heat as the cause of motion, “sanctified … above the types of motion mentioned in the books of men.” Genesis has a first motion before any other: the Spirit of God moved upon the face of the waters.
“In its absence no motion can occur, hence fire is necessary.” Jesus on what cold does: the love of many shall wax cold.

“He Who is both Stillness and Motion … out of Stillness Motion hath been engendered.” Aristotle’s first mover is itself unmoved: the final cause produces motion as being loved. How do the readings hold stillness and motion together in God, where Aristotle keeps them apart?
The contemplative traditions point the other way: be still, and know that I am God. Is the stillness the psalm asks for opposed to the motion the readings praise?
“Otherwise there is” no result. The letter to Laodicea on a community neither hot nor cold: because thou art lukewarm, I will spue thee out of my mouth.
The atoms of all things “are in perpetual motion.” Heraclitus: you cannot step twice into the same rivers; for fresh waters are ever flowing in upon you.
Wordsworth: a motion and a spirit, that impels all thinking things, all objects of all thought, and rolls through all things.

“The cause of motion is heat, and the cause of heat is the Word of God.” Psalm 147 has the whole sequence: who can stand before his cold? He sendeth out his word, and melteth them: he causeth his wind to blow, and the waters flow.
A single Word, from which came the heat that moves the universe. The last line of the Divine Comedy: the Love which moves the sun and the other stars.

bacon-heat-itself-is-motion.text: not that heat generates motion or that motion generates heat (though both are true in certain cases), but that Heat itself, its essence and quiddity, is Motion and nothing else
bacon-heat-itself-is-motion.author: Francis Bacon
